Jump in and don't worry to much about trying new things.

Read all of the text especially on the missions. I had a devil of a time doing quest until I found out they sometimes are requesting supplies not giving you them to transport and other times you need to go out and find them.

Pay your fines they will secrease your reputation. Play around will the controls and put the most used controls on the buttons closer to your hands. I use the trigger and top button on the stick for guns. The front button on the stick for target in front of you. Top right stick button for cycle targets. On the throttle the first thumb button is afterburner the second is flight assist off so I can dogfight. The last button on that side is UI focus the thumb button you have to reach for is switch weapon sets. My index finger activates supercruise in system, very usefull for running from a fight because I dont have to have a target to jump of waste fuel to jump out of the system and the reach button activates the FSD. The grey button on the base deploys hardpoints.

I have silent running on the keyboard because I rarely use that and this seems to work for me. Some if the default keybinds don't make sense. Lastly the blue bar on the throttle indicates you best turn speed. If tou really need to turn quick Flight assist off and afterburner will spin you around but remember you are in 3D space so you will not move too much so you are a sutting duck if there is more than one enemy.

Could you explain flight assist to me? I literally can't figure out what it does. I keep it on all the time, as I figured it would make life easier for a noob like me!

So flight assist make the flying more like an arcade or x-wing if you ever played that game. Turning off the throttle will slow you ship down and turning changes direction normally. With Flight assist off it works like newtonian physics. What ever vector you travel in will be affected by how you maneuver. Let say you are flying straight you can rotate the stick up and you will spin on your axis while continuing to fly forward. In fact you will continue to rotate until you counter the rotation. It is fun and useful in certain situations but I usually fly with flight assist on. one example that comes to mind if when you are docking at a station and you are coming from the side I throttle forward toward the entrance and turn FA off. I think rotate so I am facing the opening and when I am lined up I will turn FA back on and throttle forward doing a "skid" in space. Also I forgot the toggle switch you finger rests on that is on the front of the throttle I use to cycle through subsystem targeting. Usefull because bigger ships will explode if you blowup the drives or FSD even if the hull is still intact.

DnD is played on a lot of different mediums these days, from totally online to in person without even a grid. The group I'm in right now has an overhead projector which throws a screen from roll20 for maps down onto the table. There is even dynamic line-of-site built into the app so when we move our characters, our DM moves the players in roll20 and it reveals parts of the map based on our character's specific vision. In contrast, the group I'm DM'ing right now has only ever done pen & paper style. We've even had some sessions without any combat grid, just pure imagination.

So here is my question: what has been your favorite play style of DnD thus far?

My favorite so far has been around the table games. I'm most familiar with what you mentioned, pure imagination games. My longest lasting group started with other systems, like Vampire: The Masquerade, so we were always just used to that style of play where if you needed something (within reason) it was probably nearby, distances were a bit hazy (you're about 2 movement actions away kind of thing). We also did a bit of Exalted, so we enjoyed D&D with a lot more stunt battles. You hit for 8 damage is less fun than "You swing diagonally across the goblin's chest, slicing open a deep gash causing his entrails to spill to the floor."

I think roll20 is a great system, but works better for a group who starts with roll20 and doesn't start around the table. For a group that switches to it, you have a group who has a whole new system to learn, and online communication is a bit trickier than around the table. Side conversations are less distracting in person, whereas online everyone ends up at about the same volume and talking over each other. When I used roll20 originally, it was around the table and as a supplement to a tabletop map, and it was a neat addition, but still takes longer to use. To each their own though, and I know some groups prefer roll20!

I played in a game a few years ago that was old-school no miniatures or battlemat, and just descriptions of the action and layout, and I found it really frustrating. I was playing a rogue, and had a really hard time planning tactics to get into flanking without being able to see the actual layout. Now I'm playing with a group that does use miniatures, but it is pretty basic -- I supply almost all the minis and the battlemat is just an empty grid that gets dry-erase marked.

I'm intrigued by how you use roll20 around the table -- does the technology get in the way much? Does it work pretty reliably, or is there a fair bit of messing with the technology? And how is roll20 from a DM perspective -- does it require a lot of setup time, or can adventures and maps be improvised on the fly?

I can only speak from the player's perspective regarding roll20, it is our DM's setup and I've only messed with it a few times casually myself :). I'll do my best to explain how it works as well as outline the pros and cons.

Setup:
The DM has a tablet pc on the table in front of him which is logged into the DM's account on roll20. This is where he does all the work on his end, moving tokens around on the map, adjusting hit points for monsters, changing the map view, etc.

On another chrome tab he has a dummy player account logged onto roll20 which is then chromecasted to the projector which throws their "view" of the board onto the table from the ceiling. This account has a custom script on it to hide the UI in roll20 so all you see is the map and player/monster tokens.

The way it works is we put our minis on the table and the DM keeps the roll20 tokens synced up to them as we move them. From our perspective, we see the map, our tokens (covered by our minis), the enemy tokens, as well as the super awesome line of site (fog of war) on the map itself.

Pros:
* Map textures are awesome and perfect which really helps with getting immersed in the world. You can see exactly what the artist intended it to look like and the grids are indisputable.
* The dynamic line of site is probably the #1 reason for using this setup because it lets you explore a dungeon very organically. You have no idea how large it is, in which direction it goes, etc. You just have an all black screen and the areas around your character tokens revealed.
* The Initiative Tracker built into roll20 is used, but only the DM sees it. This helps keep things organized during combat and saves a lot of time when starting initiative.
* All NPC and monster stats are loaded into roll20 before a session, and he even uses the custom macros for certain attacks (if he has the time to put them in). He can move tokens around, click to roll attacks/saving throws, use macros for special actions, etc; all within a few seconds. This makes the monster/npc turns fairly fast and efficient if he spends the time preparing for it.

Cons:
* I will say that keeping our tokens synced to our minis does seem a little excessive at times. Our DM has gotten much faster at it over the months we've been playing like this and we, for the most part, don't notice anymore or have just gotten used to it. Obviously nothing is going to be faster than a player just moving their mini to wherever they want to go and having that be it, so pretty much any technology is going to slow this process down.
* Lag. Yes, lag can now happen with a tabletop game! It is not very often and in a perfect world would never happen, but in order for everything to work together it has to go over the WIFI which as we all know can just decide to take a break and move slowly sometimes.
* Disconnects. In tandem with the above, there are very rarely disconnects from the projector. This has only happened a few times and is due to the WIFI shutting down entirely.
* I suppose you could argue that the amount of multitasking required to maintain this setup while keeping a game fun/interesting is absolutely insane. This might be a good time to note that there are six players in this campaign.

Overall, I love the setup as a player but would probably jump off a cliff if I were the DM; it definitely takes the right type of person to be able to pull it off with six players. If you have any other questions about the setup feel free to ask!

From a player perspective, the fog of war stuff would be pretty neat. I think I'm pretty good about not metagaming around what my character knows about a map that I know as a player, but it seems like that feature would add a lot.

Back in the 1e and 2e days, I never played with miniatures -- at best it was dice or salt and pepper shakers on a blank table to briefly illustrate layout -- and we managed fine because we didn't know better. Once I played with minis in 3.0, there was really no going back. I imagine integrating something like roll20 would be similar.

Yeah even if you are good about not metagaming, its nice to not even have to think about it. It is much easier to think as your character about how to explore this dungeon or cave because you are legitimately exploring it yourself. If anyone has the time, tech, and money to try out the fog of war setup with roll20 I would absolutely recommend it.

I agree with you about integrating to an extent, I think it depends entirely on the players. Some folks are more into DnD as a "game" than an adventure (if that makes sense?), so going with less tech would probably be less appealing them. Whereas other players are more into the creativity and imagination of DnD, and so probably wouldn't mind going back and forth.
